Consist Generation Toolset The consist generation toolset provides a single database to store the needed details of existing and potential locomotives and rolling stock (cars). It is populated with known technologies, e.g., diesel, alternative fuels, fuel cells, and batteries. It also includes potential configurations of locomotive energy source technologies. The toolset facilitates adding new technologies or refining existing ones by guiding users to provide data compliant with the SCORE data schema. C. Energy-LTD Model The core of the SCORE toolset is the Energy-LTD (E-LTD) model that simulates the train traversing a given route as a complex rolling micro-grid of power sources and sinks, determining the optimal power flow policy in an inner loop optimization. The E-LTD models power demands, GHG emissions, stored energy consumption, and power distribution (see Fig. 2). Existing LTD models are not open source and are not tailored for exploring alternative energy trades. They are focused on the detailed transient dynamics useful for studying the coupling forces between cars and evaluating stability [4, 5, 6]. There are some commercial options available [7] but tend to be expensive (> $20k). There are also two government-funded models (TEDS*** and GTMS†††), but these are neither open-source nor readily extensible for analyzing energy alternatives. As a result, a custom, open-source LTD model was created that is based on published and well-accepted models of train dynamics. †† https://www.openrailway.org ‡‡ https://geodata.bts.gov/datasets/usdot::north-american-rail-network-lines/about §§ https://maps.gooogleapis.com/maps/api/elevation/json *** https://www.shara-associates.com/services/software.apsx ††† https://www.decisiontek.com/GTMS LTD models treat a train as a single degree of freedom system (position along the track) but with a distributed mass, to account for different elements of the consist being in curves, and on up and down grades [8]. Typical train lengths are over a mile, and include 100 cars or more in the train. The external forces modeled on the train are due to aerodynamic drag, rolling friction (which varies based on curvature), and track gradient. Note that the first is a function of velocity only and the next two are functions of position only. No external force terms are functions of time. This plays a key role in our algorithmic approach. Our model include sources and sinks for power that are used to provide the required forces experienced by the train. These sources, shown in Fig. 2, of power and energy transfer this power as a force applied to the rail. These sources are characterized with maximum rates for power and capacities for energy. Fig. 2 Power and energy sources used in SCORE. Drag forces are calculated using the Canadian National resistance model (which is an update of the traditional Davis model). The model calculates the resistance forces of a consist traveling along a route as a function of its states (position and velocity). It calculates aerodynamic drag as a function of car type or shape, rolling resistance as a function of weight, and curvature resistance or the resistance of wheels on a single axle slipping as they travel different distances traveling around a curve.
